description: A focused high-frequency Japanese kanji knowledge pack containing 200 core characters selected for broad utility across beginner and intermediate reading. The set is an instructional core, not a universal corpus ranking: exact frequency order varies by corpus, genre, and register. Each character must still be taught through verified vocabulary, readings, and sentence context.

domains.name: 200-Character High-Frequency Kanji Core
domains.description: A practical core of 200 frequently encountered and highly useful kanji for Japanese literacy instruction.

domains.name: 200-Kanji Study Method
domains.description: Progression, retrieval, vocabulary, and verification rules for teaching the core character set.

relationships.description: Every core character should be learned through verified vocabulary, context, retrieval, and review rather than isolated gloss memorization.
Year, month, day, and 午前/午後 vocabulary form a connected calendar-learning cluster.
East, west, south, and north should be taught as a directional contrast set.
Basic color kanji are best reinforced through contrast and concrete examples.
Weather, landscape, materials, and weekdays create a high-utility nature vocabulary network.
People and family kanji should be taught with relationship vocabulary and register notes.
Book, writing, language, reading, listening, and seeing connect into a practical literacy cluster.
Movement and daily routine verbs should be taught with okurigana and transitivity context.
Eating, buying, making, using, working, thinking, and knowing form a useful daily-life progression.
Electricity, vehicles, stations, roads, stores, homes, rooms, places, and locations support practical reading.
Country, city, town, village, prefecture, meetings, companies, work, matters, and things form a civic vocabulary network.
Mind, body, hand, eye, mouth, ear, foot, head, face, voice, and sound should be taught through sensory examples.
Correctness, sameness, difference, quantity, strength, goodness, and preference are best learned in semantic contrasts.
Present, reality, logic, thought, meaning, society, world, and boundary are high-value abstract reading concepts.
Question, answer, teaching, learning, testing, recording, holding, placing, beginning, and ending support instructional language.
